BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Upper-level ridging will build over the western CONUS early next week, returning dry conditions. Through the midweek, a weak upper- level shortwave will move onshore and through the Great Basin, although impacts are expected to be minimal.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Partial clearing tonight through Saturday morning.
- Widespread rain and high elevation snow late Saturday into Sunday, with the highest precipitation amounts across southern Idaho. A slight chance of thunderstorms Saturday evening.
- Cooler with gusty winds Sunday, and especially Sunday night, then drying and warming Monday through Wednesday. Slight chance of precipitation late week.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: The first of two pcpn events was exiting Idaho zones to the northeast this afternoon. This will be followed by partial clearing tonight before the next stronger system approaches Saturday. That system will include subtropical moisture, with further enhancement by a developing cold front in OR. Rain will spread northward into our CWA late Saturday, mostly on the Idaho side, and will affect our CWA strongly Saturday night through Sunday morning, with the cold front passing through Sunday morning. SPC still has a slight chance of thunderstorms Saturday afternoon and evening in southwestern Idaho. Latest model QPF has increased slightly from the previous cycle for Saturday afternoon through Sunday, with totals now estimated .40 to 80 inch in Idaho mountains, .15 to .30 inch In Idaho valleys and eastern Oregon mountains, and less than .10 inch in OR valleys. Winds will shift to northwest Sunday and increase Sunday afternoon, and especially Sunday night in the Snake Basin, possibly reaching advisory criteria east of Boise late Sunday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Upper-level ridging will build over the western CONUS early next week, returning dry conditions. Through the midweek, a weak upper- level shortwave will move onshore and through the Great Basin, although impacts are expected to be minimal. Greater impacts are expected late week when another system moves into the Pacific Northwest. Precipitation chances currently reflect some disagreement when the system will move in, but precipitation chances of 10-30% are currently forecast. Temperatures will cool slightly at higher elevations while holding nearly steady at lower elevations. Winds will generally be light through the week with patchy fog expected in valleys.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: The broad troughiness shifts east of the area sometime late Tuesday/early Wednesday with ridging replacingit, most likely for Wednesday. We expect to see a bump up in temperatures with dry conditions.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of fog again tonight across northeast and eastern Colorado.
- Unsettled weather returns late Sunday and Monday.Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during thistime. High uncertainty remains for the foothills and plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Water vapor satellite imagery showsa shortwave trough over southern California bringing widespread clouds and scattered rain showers to the Desert Southwest. Ahead of this, there is a dry slot which will result in mostly clear skies for northeast Colorado through this evening. High clouds then increase late tonight and persist through Saturday morning. At the surface, the pattern changes very little as a surface trough remains near the base of the foothills, which will help keep low level moisture in place over northeast Colorado. This will lead to another round of fog late tonight and Saturday morning. The mid and high clouds associated with the shortwave trough tracking east-northeast across the intermountain west will shift east of the area midday Saturday. Mostly sunny skies are expected during the afternoon, helping to push temperatures into the upper 50s to mid 60s across northeast Colorado.

Southwest flow aloft will increase during the day Sunday as two systems off to the west take aim at the region. The first one system, a shortwave trough moves across southern California and tracks east-northeast Sunday and Monday. This system will run ahead of the second system on Sunday, carrying subtropical moisture with it and, like many of the recent systems, bring moderate to heavy rain to the Desert Southwest and Four Corners Region. For north central and northeast Colorado, this has resulted in scattered showers over the mountains and just cloudy skies for northeast Colorado. The second system tracks eastward across Oregon and northern California Sunday and then moves across Colorado Monday. The best chance for rain and mountain snow will come late Sunday night and Monday as the main trough moves overhead. The snow level starts off high, above 11,000 feet but quickly lowers to 8,500 to 9,000 feet by Monday morning. Snow is expected to continue into Monday night when flow aloft turns north-northwesterly, a somewhat favorable direction for orographic lift across the north central mountains. Temperatures will be cool Monday due to the overhead trough and cloud cover. Northerly flow behind the trough Tuesday will keep temperatures cool with highs in the 50s with dry conditions.A few earlier model runs combined these two systems over the Central Rockies producing a strong storm system, but this scenario now looks very unlikely.

The broad troughiness shifts east of the area sometime late Tuesday/early Wednesday with ridging replacingit, most likely for Wednesday. We expect to see a bump up in temperatures with dry conditions. The ridging is expected to progress east of the area on Thursday. What replaces it is still unclear. The next upper level trough moves over the western states onThursday. Still very little model agreement on the placement, strength, and track of the upper level trough for Thursday and Friday. For the forecast, temperatures should be near normal. We will have some low PoPs in the mountains and keep the plains dry for now.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: As the high wind even diminishes on Tuesday morning, dry weather and above-average temperatures will move in for the remainder of the week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Locally dense fog is possible over portions of the High Plains Friday night into Saturday morning.
- Mild conditions are expected for Halloween (Saturday), though a few showers will be possible along and west of I-25.
- A complex but disorganized storm system will move into the area Sunday, bringing cooler temperatures and a chance for rain and high elevation snow showers.
- Widespread blustery conditions are anticipated Monday into Tuesday along and east of the Laramie range.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Expect an uneventful rest of the day as the CWA sits at the edge of an upper-level ridge to the east. Some low stratus still lingers in the Nebraska panhandle, and will likely stay through the overnight hours. Places without cloud cover are having a pleasant, mild day, with highs in the 50s and 60s. Continued light southerly flow into the overnight hours will lead to another round of likely dense fog developing overnight and continuing into Saturday morning. An area from Cheyenne to Sidney to Alliance is the most likely area to see dense fog Saturday morning, making for a spooky start to Halloween!

Areas west of the Laramie Range will likely see a showery start to Halloween as a shortwave moves across the Rockies. Hi-Res guidance has precipitation moving into Carbon County early Saturday morning and moving eastward into Albany County by mid-morning. For the most part, Hi-Res guidance shows this as the areal extent of precipitation coverage, with showers dissipating before reaching the Laramie Range. Once the stratiform precipitation dissipates, a few isolated showers could still be possible during the afternoon, but overall looks like great trick or treating weather across the forecast area. Mild temperatures will continue for Saturday with highs in the 50s and 60s. By the evening hours, temperatures will fall into the 40s and 50s, perfect temperature to keep your candy from melting! The remainder of Saturday night will be uneventful, with the potential for more fog developing in the Nebraska panhandle overnight.

Sunday has the potential to be a much wetter day as a moisture-rich trough begins to push into Wyoming. Hi-Res guidance has stratiform precipitation moving into the southwest corner of the CWA during the morning hours with precipitation gradually filling in eastward. Precipitation coverage will be greater than Saturday, with some locations likely picking up some decent rainfall amounts. However, its likely still a bit early to nail down specific rainfall amounts as synoptic models still show disorganized upper-levels with this system. This system will become more organized on Monday after it exits the forecast area.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: On Monday morning, southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska will sit in-between a surface low to the east in the Great Plains and an upper-level trough to the west over the northern Rockies. Despite the presence of nearby systems however, the day will likely start off mostly dry given a lack of favorable overlap of lift and moisture directly in our local vicinity. As Monday progresses, the upper-level trough to the west will swing eastward, and surface winds will shift out of the north. Lingering low-level moisture to the northwest of the surface low looks to get wrapped around the trough as it departs, increasing the chances of showers and possibly some snow showers to east-central Wyoming and potentially the NE panhandle. Ensemble QPF totals with the backside of this system on Monday afternoon/night still remain rather low and dispersive, similar to overnight guidance. Overall, it looks like only a tenth of an inch or so of QPF is likely east of I-25 and north of I-80. Higher amounts are possible in the northern Laramie range where favorable orographics and snowfall may last a bit longer. The other big story on Monday and Monday night will be a dramatic increase in winds on the backside of this system in the wake of a passing cold front. Ensemble guidance still is in strong support of winds possibly exceeding 50 mph, even approaching high wind criteria east of I-25 through the NE panhandle. The strongest period of high winds appears to be mid to pate afternoon, potentially over the I-80 corridor, as mixing is maximized at the time of the passage of the strongest mid-level jet aloft. The north to north-northwesterly orientation of surface flow could bring significant crosswind impacts to travelers along I-80 from the summit eastward through the high plains during this timeframe.

As the high wind even diminishes on Tuesday morning, dry weather and above-average temperatures will move in for the remainder of the week. The synoptic pattern aloft does remain fairly active, with two weak vort-maxes passing by on Tuesday night and on Wednesday night. However, both of these systems will be starved of moisture and bring only occasional increases in mid and upper-level cloud cover through the area. Forecast confidence remains relatively high through the end of the week on both above normal temperatures and drier weather. However, by the end of the week, attention will turn to a larger system with upper- level support moving through the southwestern CONUS. Ensemble guidance is quite dispersive with both the track and the amount of moisture with this event, but there is a broad consensus that Wyoming and possibly western Nebraska will see some form of precipitation from this event given its more favorable storm track bringing in southerly and southeasterly flow. We will continue to monitor this system and potential impacts with both precipitation and winter weather in the high country as we start the month of November.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: The NBM and other models have also been showing temperatures cold enough for some snow accumulation, especially over the San Juans.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Showers, maybe a few storms, move across the area late Friday night into Saturday morning. Some light snow possible at the highest elevations.
- Flooding/flash flooding concerns increase Sunday into Monday, especially for areas that have saturated soils from last week's rain. A Flood Watch remains in effect.
- Winter weather highlights have been issued for the San Juans and central mountains for accumulating snow Sunday morning through Monday evening.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: RAIN AND RAINSHOWERS RETURN FOR THE START OF THE WEEKEND:

Broad southwesterly flow continues across the area and as a shortwave trough moves through the region tomorrow, models continue to highlight some showers and storms across the CWA. This southwesterly flow will keep warm temperatures in place so most of this precipitation will fall as rain though a few inches can't be ruled out over the highest terrain of the San Juans. If stronger thunderstorms do develop, brief heavy rain may lead to some very isolated flooding issues but the bigger concern will be the push of moisture on Sunday.
WETTER, UNSETTLED, AND SNOWY SUNDAY AND MONDAY:

A robust Atmospheric River arrives on Sunday bringing well above normal amounts of moisture for this time of year across the desert southwest. Guidance continues to show precip moving into the Four Corners Sunday morning with heavier precip quickly moving in about 3 hours later as the precip spreads northeastward. This on again/off again moderate to heavier precip will continue through early Monday morning before tapering off to more showery type precip. The recent rainfall and flooding from last week is still a concern as we receive anywhere from 2 inches for the Southern Valleys and 3 to close to 4 inches of liquid precip over the San Juans. Flooding remains a concern so the Flood Watch remains in place. More in the Hydrology section below.

The NBM and other models have also been showing temperatures cold enough for some snow accumulation, especially over the San Juans. Despite snow levels increasing through the day Sunday, had enough confidence to issue a Winter Storm Watch for the San Juans for elevations above 10K feet for over a foot of snow and advisories for portions of the central mountains for 5 to 10 inches of snow, also above 10,000 feet. There is still some uncertainty in the forecast though confidence does continue to increase. Either way, please pay attention to the latest forecasts if you'll be travelling this weekend, especially over the higher terrain or the Four Corners region.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: On Mon, upper trough moves across CO, as upper low lifts out of the ern plains into ern KS by Mon evening. Showers will continue over the mountains through the day, with lowering snow levels at most locations as cold air deepens under the trough.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Scattered showers/storms along the Continental Divide tonight and Saturday morning.
- Incoming system will bring heavy rain and potential flooding to the San Juans Sunday/Sunday night, with runoff into the San Luis Valley on Monday/Tuesday.
- Snow levels drop late Sunday night, with over a foot of heavy, wet snow over the higher elevations of the ern San Juans.
- Showers elsewhere Sunday/Monday with strong winds in excess over 50 mph possible on the plains Monday behind a cold front.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: Quick update to the forecast package to include some patchy fog across portions of the eastern plains tonight.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Initial upper wave approaching the area this afternoon, with some convection firing over nrn AZ and nw NM as of 2 pm. Expect main wave of convection to pass through the area overnight (06z-12z), with a round of quick moving showers (an isolated thunderstorm possible as well), most numerous over the ern San Juans/central mountains, mainly isolated valleys and eastern mountains. QPF doesn't look particularly high, with amounts of under a quarter inch and a snow level around 9500 feet. Could also see a few showers over the far sern plains overnight, as upper low lifts out of TX, though precip here looks very light, only a few hundredths. Showers end fairly quickly Sat morning, with a lull in precip at most locations from the afternoon into Sat night. Once showers clear, Sat ends up being a very nice Autumn day (maxes in the 60s lower elevations, 40s/50s mountains), with just some moderate south winds in the afternoon as surface pressure gradient slowly tightens.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Main upper trough moves onshore Sunday morning, pushing into the Great Basin by Sunday evening, then across Colorado on Mon. Ahead of the trough, moist sw flow will develop across swrn CO, with rain starting in the ern San Juans shortly after sunrise Sun, becoming heavy from midday into the evening, then changing to snow overnight into Mon morning as colder air aloft under the upper trough moves across and mid-level flow becomes more wly. Model QPF in the San Juans continues to rise, with forecast amounts of over 3 inches of liquid near Wolf Creek Pass by Mon evening. Snow level rises to above 10000 feet by Sun afternoon, before falling back toward 9000 feet early Mon morning, which suggests the threat of several hours of rain on portions of the San Juan snowpack (SWE 1-3 inches below about 11k feet), which will increase the flooding risk. Did issue a Winter storm watch for Sun night into midday Mon for the higher elevation San Juan zone, where over a foot of snow is possible. Elsewhere, lighter showers spread across the higher terrain during the day Sun into Sun night, though precip amounts away from the San Juans will be much lighter, generally less than a half inch. Plains will stay warm and dry again on Sun, with increasing s-sw winds as surface low spins up near Limon.

On Mon, upper trough moves across CO, as upper low lifts out of the ern plains into ern KS by Mon evening. Showers will continue over the mountains through the day, with lowering snow levels at most locations as cold air deepens under the trough. Plains will see wrap-around showers and strong north winds as low departs, with heaviest precip along/south of the Arkansas River where nly upslope component will boost vertical motion. Precip ends Mon night, though north winds will remain gusty on the plains into the first half of the day Tue. Flat upper ridge then returns for most of the week from Tue onward, with warm and dry weather most locations, though next upper trough and precip are already lining up for next weekend.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: In the wake of this system, mid level ridging will bring a cool and stable airmass into the area through mid-week, followed by another series of troughs beginning Thursday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Tropical moisture will fuel showers and thunderstorms through this evening across much of Utah. Locally heavy rainfall may lead to flash flooding, particularly across southwest Utah.

- After a relative lull in precipitation on Saturday, an atmospheric river will interact with a strong cold front Sunday into Monday, resulting in widespread moderate to heavy precipitation across the region. This will increase the potential for flash flooding on Sunday across southern and eastern Utah.

- Accumulating mountain snow is expected Sunday night through early Monday as colder air spreads into the region. Local snowfall totals above 8000 feet may exceed 12" across areas favored in northwest flow.
- Cool, dry and stable conditions are expected Tuesday into Wednesday, before a more active pattern returns later next week.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: A longwave trough resides along the Pacific Coast late this morning, anchored around an upper low spinning off the WA/OR coastline near 130W. A shortwave trough is noted ejecting through the lower Colorado River Valley, and is pulling an anomalously moist airmass into the Desert Southwest/southern Great Basin. Meanwhile an Atmospheric River (AR) is noted along the base of the longwave trough near 20N. This initial shortwave passage today, followed by the main upper trough late Saturday night through Sunday, will bring 2 rounds of heavy precipitation across southern and eastern Utah. The first round this afternoon/evening will be more convective in nature, while the second round late Saturday night into Sunday associated with the inland-penetrating AR will be predominantly stratiform. See the Hydrology section below for more details on the heavy rain and flood potential through Sunday.

As the initial shortwave ejects northward, ongoing convection across southwest Utah into northern AZ will lift into central and eventually northern Utah later this afternoon through this evening. In the wake of this feature, lingering moisture will maintain a chance of showers and isolated thunderstorms Saturday, however with the forecast area remaining between today's ejecting shortwave and the approaching longwave trough axis, large scale forcing will remain limited which will keep convective coverage isolated to perhaps scattered in nature.

As the upper low off the Pacific NW coastline begins its eastward progression late Saturday, the aforementioned AR will spread inland around the southern end of the Sierra, and into the southern Great Basin/Desert Southwest Saturday night, reaching southern Utah by early Sunday. The approaching upper low will translate through the Great Basin Sunday through Sunday night, with the combination of the two bringing widespread and potentially heavy precipitation across the forecast area Sunday through Sunday night. Colder air in the wake of the surface-700mb trough axis will spread into the area late Sunday through Sunday night, with snow levels falling from 9000+ ft Sunday afternoon to below 7000 ft by early Monday. This will result in accumulating high elevation snowfall across the forecast area Sunday night through Monday morning. Assuming the post-frontal environment evolves as currently forecast, a favorable orographic setup Sunday night into Monday morning looks likely across the upper Cottonwoods and other northern/central mountains favored in NW flow, where snow totals in excess of 12" are currently forecast.

In the wake of this system, mid level ridging will bring a cool and stable airmass into the area through mid-week, followed by another series of troughs beginning Thursday. Considerable uncertainty exists regarding how this pattern evolves beyond Wednesday, thus confidence is low regarding the probability, timing and coverage of precipitation later next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: An avalanche accident on the east side of Mt. Bross highlights that you can trigger a dangerous avalanche at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) of the Central and Southern Mountains. West, north, and east-facing slopes hold multiple layers of snow from several storms in October. Deeper, wind-drifted slopes may be the most enticing for early-season snow travel, but they're also the slopes most likely to release an avalanche one to two feet deep.

Clouds build from the southwest on Friday ahead of a small initial wave of moisture. Friday night, expect light rain below around 10,000 feet, and up to six or eight inches of snow in the favored portions of the San Juan Mountains by Saturday morning, with less precipitation to the north. Saturday, the moisture tap dries out, before a stronger storm rolls in early Sunday.

On Sunday, a deep east-bound low-pressure trough brings initially warm conditions, with snow levels around 11,000 feet. Sunday night into early Monday, a cold front intensifies snowfall and pushes snow levels down to around 8,000 feet. By the end of the day Monday, expect storm totals of 1 to 2 feet of snow in the San Juan Mountains with half that amount through the Central and Northern Mountains.
Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
